Regional Overview

This volume includes all countries whose region field in the Λ¹² v2 source data is West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, or Southern Africa. The first 13 countries are the primary targets with high volatility or interest, accompanied by narrative briefings (selection is provisional and final confirmation remains with the author), while the remaining 36 countries constitute data editions sorted by η rank. All chapters follow the standard format in Section 5.2 of Volume 1.

Baseline date 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the reference list below.

Previous Trajectory

Following the dissolution of the civilian transitional government via the 2021 coup, a military-led transitional regime ensued, and in April 2023, tensions over integrating the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) escalated into a full-scale war. The office of the prime minister remained vacant after early 2022, and the government relocated to Port Sudan amid the fighting.

Direction of the Current Government

Following the recapture of the capital Khartoum in March 2025, the military-led government has shifted toward restoring administrative functions and reconstruction, including appointing a prime minister (2025-05) and returning to Khartoum (2026-01), while militarily expanding operations to retake Kordofan and Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF side has moved via the Tasis coalition to establish an independent administrative apparatus within its controlled territories, which has not been recognized by the African Union or the Arab League. Externally, the 'Quad' (Saudi Arabia, the United States, Egypt, and the UAE) is mediating a ceasefire roadmap.

Chronology 2024~2026

  • 2025-04The RSF launched a massive assault on Zamzam, the largest displaced persons camp in North Darfur, displacing over 400,000 people.[11]
  • 2025-05-19Army Commander-in-Chief Burhan appointed former UN official Kamil Idris as prime minister (the first prime ministerial appointment since the 2021 coup).[5][6]
  • 2025-07-26The RSF-led Tasis coalition announced the establishment of a parallel government, with Dagalo chairing a 15-member presidential council and al-Taishi serving as prime minister.[2][3][4]
  • 2025-07-29The African Union Peace and Security Council and the Arab League rejected the RSF-led parallel government and urged member states not to recognize it.[3][4]
  • 2025-10-26After an 18-month siege, the RSF seized El Fasher, the state capital of North Darfur.[8][11]
  • 2025-12-04A drone attack on a kindergarten and hospital in Kologi, South Kordofan, killed 114 people, including 63 children.[8]
  • 2026-01-11The prime minister announced the government's return to Khartoum, concluding an approximately three-year stay in Port Sudan.[9]
  • 2026-02The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) released a report stating that at least 6,000 people were killed over three days in El Fasher in late October 2025.[10]
  • 2026-06-19UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned of an imminent RSF offensive on El Obeid, North Kordofan, urging an immediate halt.[12]

Public Trends

Unverifiable (Scope of collected sources: reports from 2025-05 to 2026-06; reports related to collective actions such as protests and strikes under wartime conditions were not collected).

Discrepancies in Figures

Sudanese government official casualty figures are unverifiable. El Fasher (2025-10-25~27): Per OHCHR, 4,400 in the city + over 1,600 during displacement, totaling at least 6,000 (OHCHR itself noted the actual toll is 'substantially higher'). Displaced persons: Al Jazeera reported 11 million IDPs vs. Arab News reporting 'more than 12 million displaced' (presumed difference regarding inclusion of cross-border refugees, but unverifiable). Hunger: Al Jazeera reported 'over 33 million facing hunger' vs. Arab News reporting '30 million in need of aid' (different indicator definitions). The military's claim of 'destroying approximately 240 combat vehicles' remains a unilateral assertion contested by the RSF.

Data Caveats

Due to the depletion of web search quotas, this briefing could not verify developments from 2026-07 to October (progress in Quad negotiations, front-line shifts, Prime Minister Idris's continued tenure). Battlefield claims made by the combatants are frequently contested, and systematic official statistics for nationwide casualties are unavailable.

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of StatePresident Taye Atske SelassieUnconfirmed (outside collected sources; tenure following the inauguration of the new parliament in 2026-10 unconfirmed)Unconfirmed
Head of GovernmentPrime Minister Abiy Ahmed2018 (Sworn in for second five-year term on 2026-10-05)Prosperity Party

As of 2026-10-07 · Compiled from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

After coming to power in 2018, Prime Minister Abiy ended hostilities with Eritrea and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. The 2020–2022 Tigray War was halted by the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, and the Prosperity Party won 410 of 484 seats in the 2021 general election. Since 2023, the Fano militia has seized substantial rural areas in the Amhara region.

Current Government Direction

Following a landslide victory in the 2026-06-01 general election, the administration inaugurated the 'Medemer Government' on 2026-10-05, emphasizing continuity with its existing statecraft philosophy. Externally, sparked by claims to Red Sea access, it is pivoting from the 2018 reconciliation line with Eritrea toward severing diplomatic relations; regarding Tigray, amid the unraveling of the Pretoria Agreement framework, it is shifting toward federal troop redeployment and military responses.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2026-02Federal troops were deployed toward Tigray near the Eritrean border, followed by an increase in Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) attacks in the Oromia region.[1]
  • 2026-02-08The Ethiopian government publicly condemned Eritrea's military aggression and support for armed groups (reported by Reuters, via secondary sources).[4]
  • 2026-05The TPLF reconstituted the pre-war regional legislative council and elected Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president, clashing with the federally appointed Interim Regional Administration led by Taddesse Worede.[1][2]
  • 2026-06The Prosperity Party secured victory by winning 438 of 486 seats in the House of Peoples' Representatives (AFP; approximately 40 million voted out of about 54 million registered voters).[3]
  • 2026-06-01General elections were held; Tigray was excluded from voting, and several constituencies in Amhara (at least eight) also could not vote due to security issues.[2][3]
  • 2026-09-23Fighting resumed in Tigray, and the TPLF withdrew from Mekelle citing risk to civilians, though airstrikes and artillery shelling continued in other areas.[5]
  • 2026-10-01Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, and Eritrea announced the severance of diplomatic relations the following day (Ethiopia alleged Eritrean backing of the TPLF, which Eritrea denied).[5][7]
  • 2026-10-05Prime Minister Abiy took the oath of office for a second five-year term at the first session of the 7th House of Peoples' Representatives.[5][6]

Public Trends

In the 2026-06 general election, Fano in Amhara warned that election participants would be regarded as 'enemies of the Amhara people.' The opposition was fragmented, and while over 40 parties ran, most were reported to lack financial backing. Reports of large-scale urban protests or strikes were not identified within the monitoring window (reports from 2026-05 to 2026-10).

Discrepancies in Figures

Total parliamentary seats: AFP affiliate report (The Standard) 438 out of 486 seats vs. Africanews 438 out of 547 seats (likely the difference between total statutory seats and seats contested, but unconfirmed). Election date: Arab News states 'Monday (around 5-27)', while Chatham House and AFP describe it as 2026-06-01 — this briefing adopts 2026-06-01. Fatalities near Mekelle: Capital FM reports 'at least 17', Africanews video caption '52' (may differ by timing and locality). Official government casualty counts are unconfirmed. Tigray hostilities (2026-09–): AFP reports 'hundreds of casualties', medical aid groups tallied over 420 wounded through 9-25.

Data Caveats

Official National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) result documents and the exact date of diplomatic severance with Eritrea were not directly verified. 2025–2026 developments regarding economic reforms (IMF program, Birr exchange rate liberalization) were not gathered due to search constraints. Information regarding Tigray fighting has limited independent verification.

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of State and Head of GovernmentPresident Isaias Afwerki1993 (Since independence)People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ, sole legal party)

As of 2026-10-07 · Compiled from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

Eritrea suspended its activities in the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) in 2007 in protest against support for Ethiopia's intervention in Somalia, faced UN sanctions in 2009, which were lifted after normalizing relations with Ethiopia in 2018. It rejoined IGAD in 2023-06 but subsequently did not participate in its meetings or initiatives. Domestically, human rights organizations have noted that an indefinite national service system and the prohibition of independent media, civil society, and opposition parties have been maintained.

Current Government Direction

It is pivoting toward withdrawing from regional multilateral organizations (formally withdrawing from IGAD in 2025-12) and demanding the termination of the UN Human Rights Council Special Rapporteur monitoring mandate. Characterizing Ethiopia's claims to Red Sea access as an 'incessant hostile agenda,' it responded to Ethiopia's embassy closure in 2026-10 by severing diplomatic relations.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-06Eritrea submitted a resolution to the UN Human Rights Council to terminate the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on its country (result unconfirmed).[2]
  • 2025-12-12Eritrea formally withdrew from IGAD, stating that it 'abdicates its legal obligations and serves as an instrument contrary to its interests.'[1]
  • 2026-02Ethiopia deployed troops toward Tigray near the Eritrean border, and the Ethiopian government condemned Eritrea's aggression and support for armed groups.[3][4]
  • 2026-09Hostilities resumed in Tigray between the TPLF and federal forces, with Ethiopia alleging that Eritrea was supporting the TPLF.[5]
  • 2026-10-01Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats.[5][6]
  • 2026-10-02Eritrea announced the severance of all diplomatic relations with Ethiopia.[5][6]

Public Trends

Because independent media, civil society, and opposition activities are not permitted in Eritrea, there are no reports concerning domestic collective action (monitoring window: reports from 2025-06 to 2026-10). Human rights reports indicate the continuation of indefinite national service and punishment of draft evaders.

Data Caveats

Eritrea does not regularly publish national statistics or budgets, and is reported to have never accepted a visit by independent UN human rights experts. The result of the 2025-07 Human Rights Council vote and the scale of Eritrean military operations inside Tigray could not be confirmed due to search limits. The year of the head of state's assumption of office was not directly verified through collected sources.

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTerm BeganAffiliation
Head of StatePresident Félix Tshisekedi2019-01 (Second term scheduled to end in 2028)Ruling coalition led by the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS)
Head of GovernmentPrime Minister Judith SuminwaUnverifiable (outside the scope of collected sources; 2026 incumbency unconfirmed)Unverifiable

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the reference list below.

Previous Trajectory

In 2025, M23 rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, and Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu, while the Congolese government has accused Rwanda of backing M23. Under US mediation, the Washington Peace Agreement of 2025-06-27 and the Washington Agreement for Peace and Prosperity of 2025-12-04 were signed, and the Doha Framework between the government and M23/AFC was signed on 2025-11-15 during the Qatar-mediated Doha Process.

Direction of the Current Government

Externally, within the framework of implementing the Washington Agreement, the government is moving toward a 'negotiated disarmament' approach for certain factions of the FDLR, which Rwanda rejects by demanding 'neutralisation'. Through the Critical Minerals Framework with the US (2025-12), it is pivoting toward attracting US corporate investments. Domestically, it is moving toward opening constitutional amendment procedures through the enactment of a Referendum Act (passed parliament in 2026-06, followed by conditional approval by the Constitutional Court in 2026-07 and the president's subsequent request for parliamentary review).

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-06-27The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda signed a peace agreement in Washington, D.C.[1]
  • 2025-11-15The Congolese government and M23/AFC signed the Doha Framework under Qatari mediation.[1]
  • 2025-12Uvira in South Kivu fell following an offensive by M23 and Rwandan forces, immediately after which the Washington Agreement was reaffirmed and signed on 2025-12-04 (including the US–DRC Critical Minerals Framework).[1][2]
  • 2026-03-02The US Department of the Treasury sanctioned the Rwandan military leadership, and the Department of State announced visa restrictions on high-ranking officials on 2026-03-06.[2]
  • 2026-06The Organic Law on the Organization of Referendums passed the Senate following the National Assembly, and a local human rights group stated it recovered two bodies following clashes between pro- and anti-referendum rallies (AFP).[3]
  • 2026-07-28The Congolese government announced the acceptance of disarmament procedures for an FDLR faction, but Rwanda rejected this, demanding neutralization.[1]
  • 2026-07-28The Constitutional Court approved the Referendum Act with interpretative reservations (reported as 7-28 or 7-29), after which President Tshisekedi requested parliament to review the bill.[4][5]
  • 2026-09-15The opposition coalition C64 (Fayulu, Katumbi, Kabund, Matata Ponyo, Sesanga, etc.) held an 'Anti-Third Term' march in Kinshasa, and authorities rerouted the march (hundreds of participants reported).[6]
  • 2026-09-16A two-day meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) under the Washington Agreement was held in Geneva.[1]

Public Trends

The opposition coalition C64 opposed amending constitutional provisions on presidential terms (Articles 70 and 220), holding a 'ghost town' general strike in early 2026-06; after the 8-15 deadline requesting an inclusive national dialogue with President Tshisekedi passed, it held a march of several hundred people in Kinshasa on 2026-09-15 (rallies were banned in certain areas such as Lubumbashi). On 2026-07-17, Cardinal Ambongo conveyed the president's willingness to engage in national dialogue.

Discrepancies in Figures

Casualties in pro/anti-rallies in 2026-06: Local human rights groups claimed to have recovered 2 bodies; no official government figures released. Casualty and displacement figures for the eastern conflict are unverifiable from the collected sources. Referendum Act approval date by the Constitutional Court: Afrik.com reported 7-28 vs. La Libre reported 7-29.

Data Warnings

The schedule for holding the referendum, the outcome of the Geneva JSCM meeting, and the Prime Minister's incumbency could not be confirmed due to search limits. In eastern conflict areas, an M23 parallel administration operates, leaving them out of reach for government statistics. Claims regarding the FDLR conflict between the two governments' positions.

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTerm BeganAffiliation
Head of State and GovernmentPresident Bola Tinubu2023-05All Progressives Congress (APC)

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the reference list below.

Previous Trajectory

Upon taking office in 2023, the Tinubu administration abolished the fuel subsidy, which had cost approximately $10 billion annually, and unified the official and parallel exchange rates, leading to a sharp depreciation of the naira. The inflation rate surged to approximately 35% in 2024, and during the crackdown on the '#EndBadGovernance' protests in 2024-08, more than 1,000 people were arrested and at least 24 were killed.

Direction of the Current Government

The government is pivoting toward expanding non-oil tax revenue through a centralized new tax system, and inflation dropped from an average of about 23% in 2025 to 15% in early 2026. In terms of security, it is accommodating counterterrorism cooperation with the United States (US airstrikes in 2025-12, deployment of approximately 200 US military personnel for training and advisory roles in early 2026). Politically, with multiple opposition (PDP) governors joining the ruling party, a consolidation around the ruling party is underway ahead of the 2027-01-16 presidential and general elections.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2024-08Over 1,000 people were arrested and at least 24 were killed in the crackdown on the '#EndBadGovernance' protests.[1]
  • 2025President Tinubu declared a six-month state of emergency in Rivers State, citing pipeline vandalism, among other reasons.[1]
  • 2025-10The government uncovered a coup plot, arresting 16 officers and indicting 6; in the same month, the US Department of State designated Nigeria as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC) for religious freedom.[1]
  • 2025-11Twenty-five schoolgirls were abducted from a school in Kebbi State, and a few days later, more than 300 individuals were abducted from a Catholic school in Niger State.[1]
  • 2025-12The United States issued a proclamation suspending the entry of Nigerian citizens under most visa categories.[1]
  • 2025-12-25The United States conducted airstrikes targeting Islamic State (IS) forces in Nigeria.[1]
  • 2026-01The United States introduced a visa bond requirement for Nigerian citizens.[1]
  • 2026-02-26The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) rescheduled the presidential and general elections to 2027-01-16 and the gubernatorial and state assembly elections to 2027-02-06, citing the enactment of the 'Electoral Act 2026' and overlapping Ramadan schedules.[2]
  • 2026-04-28James Faleke, a pro-Tinubu lawmaker, purchased the APC presidential nomination forms for 100 million naira, marking President Tinubu's entry into the re-election bid process (APC primary scheduled for 2026-05-15–16).[3]
  • 2026-05-27In the opposition ADC primary, Atiku Abubakar was elected presidential candidate with over 1.84 million votes, while in the ruling APC primary, President Tinubu became the candidate with approximately 10.9 million votes.[4][5]

Public Trends

The most recent nationwide mass protest reported was the '#EndBadGovernance' protest in 2024-08. No large-scale collective actions were reported in 2026 within the monitored scope (reports from 2026-02 to 07). Ahead of the 2027-01-16 presidential election, party primaries in 2026-05 confirmed Tinubu (APC) and Atiku Abubakar (ADC) as candidates, while Peter Obi was slated for nomination by the NDC; allegations of vote manipulation and electoral law violations surfaced during the primary process.

Discrepancies in Figures

Allegations of 'Christian massacres': A divergence in positions exists where the US side (Trump administration) defined it as religious persecution and designated Nigeria as a CPC, whereas the Nigerian government explains it as armed violence affecting multiple religious groups (official government casualty statistics unverifiable). The change in debt-to-GDP ratio from 53% (2024) to 32% (2026) reflects the impact of GDP rebasing.

Data Warnings

Developments after 2026-07 (Obi's confirmation as NDC candidate, security incidents) could not be verified due to search limits. Casualty statistics in northern conflict zones vary in tallying methodology depending on the source. In 2026, the food-insecure population stood at approximately 36 million, with over 3.7 million internally displaced persons (citing CRS). Reports on INEC schedules listed the party primary period as '2027-04-23–05-30', which appears to be a clerical error for 2026 as it conflicts with the election date (2027-01) (original text unverifiable).

4. Situation Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of State and Head of GovernmentPresident William Ruto2022-09United Democratic Alliance (UDA)-led ruling coalition; 'broad-based' cooperation framework with ODM since 2025-03

Base date 2026-10-07 · Gathered from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

The Ruto administration pursued tax hikes amid rising costs of living; in 2024-06, youth (Gen Z) protesters opposing the Finance Bill breached parliament, and police firing triggered domestic and international condemnation. Later, in 2025-03, he signed the '10-point agenda' with opposition leader Raila Odinga, establishing a broad-based cooperation framework.

Direction of the Current Government

Heading into the 2027-08 general elections, the government is pivoting toward coalition politics by expanding alliances with the ODM (2025-03), KANU (2025-10), and others. In handling protests, while recognizing the right to demonstrate, it combines stern warnings and massive police deployments against property destruction and civil unrest, while simultaneously pushing forward a compensation program for approximately 1,100 victims of protest violence.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2024-06-25Gen Z-led protesters opposing tax hikes breached parliament, and police opened fire.[1][2]
  • 2025-03-07President Ruto and Raila Odinga signed a '10-point agenda', launching a broad-based cooperation framework.[3]
  • 2025-06Blogger Albert Ojwang died in police custody, and 21 people were killed in protests on 2025-06-25 (KNCHR).[3][4]
  • 2025-07-0732 people died during Saba Saba protests, marking the highest single-day death toll (KNCHR).[4]
  • 2025-10-10President Ruto and KANU leader Gideon Moi announced a political alliance aimed at the 2027 general elections.[3]
  • 2025-10-19Former Prime Minister Raila Odinga died at age 80 while receiving medical treatment in India; subsequently, Senator Oburu Oginga was elected ODM leader.[3]
  • 2025-11-27By-elections were conducted in Malaba, Mbeere North, and other constituencies under the reconstituted Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) system.[3]
  • 2026-06-25On the 2nd anniversary of the Gen Z protests, memorial and justice-demanding marches were held in Nairobi amid police cordons.[1][2]

Public Trends

Since 2024-06, youth-led anti-government protests have recurred annually, centered around June 25 and Saba Saba (July 7). In the 2nd anniversary protests on 2026-06-25, protesters demanded justice, compensation, and investigations for victims of police violence, while former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua urged youth to 'stay home.' The next general election is scheduled for 2027-08.

Discrepancies in Figures

Protest fatalities: At least 127 over 2 years (2024–2026) recorded by police watchdog agencies (cited by AFP); 115 from 2024-06 to 2025-07 recorded by KNCHR (62 from 2024-06 to 2025-02, 21 on 2025-06-25, 32 on 2025-07-07). Official government (Interior Ministry/Police) death toll figures could not be confirmed.

Data Caution

Casualty and arrest numbers on 2026-06-25 and trends during the 2026-07 Saba Saba were not confirmed in gathered sources. The contents of the 2026 Finance Bill and IMF-related developments could not be verified due to search limitations.

4. Situation Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of State (Transitional)Colonel Michael Randrianirina2025-10-17 (Inauguration oath)Military-led transitional government
Head of GovernmentPrime Minister Mamitiana Jeannot Ruffin Rajaonarison2026-03 (Appointment reported as 3-15 or 3-16)Independent (Former Director-General of Financial Intelligence Unit SAMIFIN)

Base date 2026-10-07 · Gathered from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

During President Andry Rajoelina's administration, job shortages and tap water and electricity outages accumulated; in 2025-09, youth (Gen Z)-led protests began and escalated into nationwide anti-government demonstrations. After military units defected to join the protesters, President Rajoelina departed the country on 2025-10-11–12, and parliament impeached him on 10-14 for dereliction of duty.

Direction of the Current Government

The Randrianirina transitional government denies the coup designation, claiming it 'received' power from the High Constitutional Court, and is oriented toward drafting a new constitution and holding presidential elections in late 2027 in accordance with the two-year transition roadmap (announced in late 2026-02). Following the replacement of the prime minister and cabinet in 2026-03, it is pivoting toward emphasizing 'swift, tangible socioeconomic results' by appointing an anti-corruption and financial intelligence expert as prime minister.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-09Youth-led protests against water and power shortages began and escalated into anti-government demonstrations.[1][2]
  • 2025-10-11President Rajoelina departed the country citing threats to his life (reported heading to Dubai via Réunion with French assistance).[2]
  • 2025-10-14Parliament impeached Rajoelina for dereliction of duty, and the Supreme Court approved it.[2][3]
  • 2025-10-17Colonel Randrianirina took the oath of office as president, and the African Union (AU) suspended Madagascar's membership.[2]
  • 2025-10Private sector entrepreneur Herintsalama Rajaonarivelo was appointed prime minister.[1]
  • 2026-02A two-year transition roadmap was unveiled, presenting a timeline for national consultations and a new constitution by late 2026, followed by presidential elections in late 2027.[1]
  • 2026-03-11Randrianirina dismissed Prime Minister Rajaonarivelo and dissolved the cabinet (reasons undisclosed).[1]
  • 2026-03-16Director-General of the Financial Intelligence Unit (SAMIFIN) Mamitiana Rajaonarison was appointed as new prime minister.[3][4]

Public Trends

The Gen Z protests of 2025-09–10 led to regime change. Since then, whether the Gen Z movement participates in the transitional government and any large-scale collective actions after 2026-03 could not be confirmed within the surveyed scope (reports up to 2026-03).

Discrepancies in Figures

2025 protest casualties: UN tally records at least 22 dead and over 100 injured (cited by CBS); official government numbers could not be confirmed. New prime minister appointment date: Wikipedia records 3-15, Ecofin records 3-16.

Data Caution

Trends from 2026-04 to 10 (constitutional draft, lifting of AU suspension, economic indicators) could not be verified due to search limitations. Transitional government legitimacy (whether it constitutes a coup) involves conflicting characterizations between the parties.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of State and Head of GovernmentPresident Hakainde Hichilema2021-08 (Inauguration for 2nd term 2026-09-01)United Party for National Development (UPND)

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from open sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

During his first term (2021–2026), President Hichilema was reported to have pursued national debt restructuring, attracted international investment, and curbed inflation. Following the death of former President Edgar Lungu in South Africa in 2025-06, a legal dispute ensued between the government and the bereaved family over the funeral and burial site, which was reported to reflect the long-standing political rivalry between the two.

Current Government Direction

Following his reelection in the presidential election on 2026-08-13, the second administration took office, and the government is oriented toward judicial prosecution regarding allegations of treason and armed militia activity against the opposition candidate's camp. In the economic realm, it is reported to continue the first term's line of debt restructuring and investment attraction, but specific policy announcements for the second term cannot be confirmed.

Chronology 2024~2026

  • 2025-06-05Former President Edgar Lungu passed away at age 68 while undergoing treatment for heart disease in Pretoria, South Africa.[1]
  • 2025-08-08The South African High Court ruled in favor of the Zambian government to repatriate Lungu's remains to Zambia for a state funeral.[1]
  • 2026The Supreme Court of Appeal of South Africa (SCA) upheld the bereaved family's right to bury him in South Africa, and the Zambian government accepted the ruling, concluding the legal dispute (exact ruling date unconfirmed).[2]
  • 2026-08-13In the presidential election, President Hichilema won approximately 60% of the vote, while candidate Brian Mundubile of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance garnered around 38%.[3][4][5]
  • 2026-08Former Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed during a police raid on Mundubile's residence, and police arrested 11 individuals, alleging involvement in 'rebellion and militia activities.'[4]
  • 2026-08-24On the deadline for filing election petitions, the government closed courts nationwide citing 'security reasons,' preventing any election petition from being filed with the Constitutional Court.[4][5]
  • 2026-08-27Candidate Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu, who had been in hiding for two weeks, turned themselves in and were detained on treason charges (reported as 'Thursday').[3][4]
  • 2026-09-01President Hichilema took the oath of office for his second term at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka.[6]

Public Trends

The opposition raised issues over the deployment of military personnel to polling stations and requested intervention from the African Union (AU), while some independent monitoring groups alleged signs of incumbent vote inflation (names of monitoring groups unconfirmed). Human Rights Watch criticized the court closures as a measure 'without credible explanation.' Reports of large-scale street protests were not gathered within the monitored scope (reports from 2026-08 to 09).

Discrepancies in Figures

The original text of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) official vote shares could not be verified; media (AFP, etc.) reported approximately 60% for Hichilema vs. approximately 38% for Mundubile. The opposition and some monitoring groups alleged that the incumbent's tally was inflated (figures not presented).

Data Caution

Official ECZ results, voter turnout, the progress of treason trials, and IMF program trends after 2026-09 could not be confirmed due to search limits. The date of the South African SCA ruling is also unconfirmed.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateGeneral and President Abdourahamane Tiani2023-07 (Assumed power after detaining President Mohamed Bazoum)Military government; Alliance of Sahel States (AES)
Head of GovernmentUnconfirmedUnconfirmedUnconfirmed

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from open sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

After the military detained President Bazoum and took power in 2023-07, it withdrew French forces in 2023-12 and initiated a review of foreign mining concessions. France's Orano halted production at the Somaïr uranium mine in 2024-10, and the military government seized operational control in 2024-12. It formed the AES with Mali and Burkina Faso in 2023-09 and withdrew from ECOWAS in 2025-01.

Direction of the Current Government

It is shifting toward strengthening resource sovereignty, pursuing direct sales of uranium on the international market following the nationalization of Somaïr in 2025-06; however, the government stated that sales did not materialize due to legal disputes, including international arbitration (ICSID) initiated by Orano (2026-05). In terms of security, it operates through cooperation with 'Russian partners' and the AES joint military framework.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-01Niger completed its withdrawal from ECOWAS alongside Mali and Burkina Faso (exact date unverified from collected sources).[6]
  • 2025-06The military government announced the nationalization of the Somaïr mine (owned 63.4% by Orano and 36.6% by the state-owned Sopamin), and Orano characterized this as 'expropriation' and announced legal action.[1]
  • 2025-12A joint military force and the Sahel Investment and Development Bank were launched at the Bamako AES Summit.[6]
  • 2026-01-29The Islamic State (IS) attacked Niamey's Diori Hamani International Airport and airbase; the military announced that 20 attackers were killed and 4 soldiers wounded (reported as 'Thursday').[2]
  • 2026-01-30President Tiani claimed to have repelled the attack alongside 'Russian partners' and accused the presidents of France, Benin, and Côte d'Ivoire of sponsoring the attack.[2]
  • 2026-05-05The Minister of Mines stated that uranium (approx. 1,800 tons, worth approx. 380 million USD) could not be sold following nationalization, and that an ICSID ruling was preventing inventory disposal.[3]
  • 2026-08-29Soldiers from a Niamey base staged a mutiny attacking the airport and presidential palace, but state television announced that it was suppressed (Reuters).[4][5]

Public Trends

Reports of large-scale anti-government protests in 2026 were not collected within the scope of review (2026-01–09 reports); an internal military mutiny occurred in Niamey on 2026-08-29.

Numerical Discrepancies

2026-01 airport attack: Government (military) announced 20 attackers killed and 4 soldiers wounded; IS claimed 'significant damage.' Uranium dispute: Niger's government stated that Orano filed at least 10 lawsuits, whereas Orano stated 4 arbitrations, showing a discrepancy. Official casualty figures for the 2026-08 mutiny cannot be verified.

Data Caveats

Cabinet composition including the Prime Minister, the 2025 Transitional Charter (term extension, party dissolution status), and post-mutiny handling results following 2026-08 could not be verified due to search limitations. The military government restricts press access, limiting independent verification.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of State (Transitional President)General Assimi Goïta2021 (military-led government following 2020 and 2021 coups)Military transitional government; Alliance of Sahel States (AES)
Head of GovernmentUnidentifiableUnidentifiableUnidentifiable

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

Mali has been governed by a military government following coups in 2020 and 2021; French troops were fully withdrawn in 2022, and French state broadcasters were banned. The military government severed defense cooperation with France and the US, pivoting toward security cooperation with Russia (Africa Corps). It formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) with Burkina Faso and Niger in 2023-09 and withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 2025-01.

Direction of the Current Government

Within the AES confederation framework, it is shifting toward regional integration through a joint military force and the Sahel Investment and Development Bank; externally, in addition to Russia, it is moving toward restoring relations with Algeria (Algerian Prime Minister's visit in 2026-09, preparations for Goïta's visit to Algeria). In terms of security, it maintains a military-escorted fuel convoy system in response to JNIM's fuel blockade.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-01Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger officially withdrew from ECOWAS.[5]
  • 2025-08The government arrested two generals and dozens of soldiers on charges of plotting state destabilization (Reuters).[1]
  • 2025-09JNIM began a fuel blockade of Bamako by attacking fuel convoys from Côte d'Ivoire and Senegal, resulting in school closures and power shortages.[1][2]
  • 2025-12The 2nd AES Summit in Bamako launched a joint military force, the Sahel Investment and Development Bank, and a joint TV channel, with the rotating presidency passing from Goïta to Traoré.[2]
  • 2026-04-25JNIM and the Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) launched simultaneous attacks on the Bamako airport/airbase, Kati base, Kidal, Gao, and Mopti; the government declared a 3-day night curfew.[3]
  • 2026-04-30FLA claimed control of the Tessalit Amachach base, JNIM claimed control of the Hombori base, and checkpoints set up around Bamako were reported (Russian Africa Corps refuted JNIM's claims).[4]
  • 2026-09-10JNIM attacked the Dioura military base in central Mali, killing at least 50 soldiers and 5 Russian Africa Corps personnel.[6]
  • 2026-09-14JNIM attacked a military-escorted fuel convoy (over 80 tankers) en route to Bamako from Senegal, setting approx. 20 on fire.[6]

Public Trends

Support rallies were reported across the three countries at the time of the ECOWAS withdrawal in 2025-01. Although school closures and commercial paralysis occurred following the fuel blockade after 2025-09, reports of large-scale anti-government protests were not collected within the scope of review (2025-11–2026-09 reports). JNIM urged the Malian public to 'overthrow the junta' and adopt Islamic law in 2026-04.

Numerical Discrepancies

2026-04-25 attack: Government official announcement of 16 wounded and 'multiple' militants killed (death toll not released). Defense Minister Sadio Camara: Al Jazeera reported he was killed in the 2026-04 attack, whereas AP reported only that his residence was heavily damaged by an explosion on that day — official government confirmation cannot be verified. Dioura attack (2026-09-10): At least 50 dead vs. some sources reporting 60–80; the Malian military released only the outcomes of retaliatory airstrikes.

Data Caveats

The government's battlefield damage announcements are limited, and claims by JNIM/FLA conflict with Russian refutations. Details regarding the Prime Minister, Goïta's 2025 term extension, and the blockade status from 2026-05 to 08 could not be verified due to search limitations.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of State and Head of GovernmentPresident Cyril Ramaphosa2018-02 (Re-elected after 2024 general election)African National Congress (ANC)-led Government of National Unity (GNU)

Reference date 2026-10-07 · Compiled from open sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

In the 2024 general election, the ANC lost its sole majority with around 40% of the vote and formed a Government of National Unity (GNU) with the Democratic Alliance (DA), Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), and others. In 2025, coalition friction continued, including DA threats to withdraw over a VAT increase (2025-02) and the dismissal of a DA-affiliated deputy minister (2025-06). In relations with the US, even after a summit (2025-05), the US boycotted the G20 Summit in November.

Current Government Direction

The government is maintaining the GNU coalition framework while preparing for the 2026-11-04 local government elections, emphasizing improved service delivery and increased youth voter turnout. Coalition partner DA, following a leadership change (2026-04), is shifting direction such that the new federal leader participates in the GNU via proxies rather than serving directly in the cabinet. Economically, the focus is on driving growth recovery after removal from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) grey list (2025-10).

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-02The DA threatened to exit the GNU following a VAT increase announcement, but President Ramaphosa brokered a compromise.[1]
  • 2025-05President Ramaphosa met President Trump at the White House to discuss trade, farm attacks, and land reform issues.[1]
  • 2025-06President Ramaphosa dismissed DA-affiliated Deputy Minister Andrew Whitfield citing an unauthorized visit to the US.[1]
  • 2025-10South Africa was removed from the FATF grey list.[2]
  • 2025-11Africa's first G20 Summit was held in Johannesburg; the US did not attend.[1]
  • 2025-12The ANC National General Council (NGC) concluded, reaffirming support for Ramaphosa's leadership.[1]
  • 2026-04-12Cape Town Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis was elected DA Federal Leader with over 90% of the vote (John Steenhuisen had announced in 2026-02 that he would not run).[3]
  • 2026-04-30President Ramaphosa proclaimed 2026-11-04 as the date for the local government elections.[4]

Public Trends

Within the confirmed monitoring scope (reports from 2025-12 to 2026-04), no reports of large-scale nationwide protests or strikes were collected. Ahead of the 2026-11-04 local elections, the MK Party led by Jacob Zuma is seeking to expand its influence based on its 2024 electoral gains, while the president urged higher youth voter turnout.

Data Caution

Economic indicators (Q3 2025 growth rate 0.5%, unemployment rate 33%, government debt over 70% of GDP) are media-cited figures; primary data from Statistics South Africa (Stats SA) were not directly verified. US tariff and diplomatic relations and the progress of the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry between 2026-05 and 2026-10 could not be confirmed due to search limits.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StatePresident Hassan Sheikh Mohamud2022-05 (Original term expiration 2026-05-15, extended by 1 year via constitutional amendment)Unverifiable
Head of GovernmentUnverifiable (Prime minister's name not specified in collected sources)UnverifiableUnverifiable

Reference date 2026-10-07 · Compiled from open sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

Somalia had elected its president through indirect elections by clan representatives, and restored the principle of universal suffrage for the 2026 elections via a 2024 legal amendment (direct election of legislators, parliamentary election of the president). On 2025-04-23, voter registration began for the first time in about 50 years. Puntland and Jubaland leadership alongside the opposition formed the 'Somali Future Council' in opposition to the federal government's electoral procedures.

Current Government Direction

Citing the introduction of a one-person-one-vote direct election system and the 'completion' of the constitution, the federal government shifted course by extending the presidential and parliamentary terms from 4 to 5 years and delaying elections by 1 year (2026-03). Externally, it is focusing on territorial integrity diplomacy through the UN Security Council, AU, and Arab League in response to Israel's recognition of Somaliland. Dialogue continues with the opposition over election management bodies and voting modalities, but no agreement had been reached as of 2026-09.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-04-23Voter registration commenced for the first time in over 50 years.[3]
  • 2025-12-26Israel recognized Somaliland as a state, and the AU condemned it within 48 hours.[4]
  • 2025-12-29At an emergency UN Security Council meeting convened at Somalia's request, most member states except the US voiced opposition to the recognition (reported as 'Monday').[4]
  • 2026-03-05Parliament passed a constitutional amendment with 222 votes across both houses to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from 4 to 5 years and postpone the scheduled 2026-05 election by 1 year (Reuters).[1]
  • 2026-05-15President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's original term expired; the opposition claimed the extension was unconstitutional.[2][3]
  • 2026-06-04Nighttime clashes broke out in Mogadishu between government forces and opposition armed groups; UN Secretary-General Guterres urged restraint and resumption of dialogue.[2][5]
  • 2026-09-23The opposition stated that government–opposition (Somali Future Council) electoral talks concluded without agreement on core issues such as election management bodies and voting modalities.[6]

Public Trends

Ahead of planned opposition protests in early 2026-06, firefights erupted in Mogadishu, and opposition leaders including former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire and former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed criticized the government. Former presidents and prime ministers opposed the 2026-03 constitutional amendment and demanded the holding of elections in May as scheduled.

Discrepancies in Figures

Casualties from the 2026-06 Mogadishu clashes: No official tally; local reports only mentioned mortar-inflicted injuries and property damage. Somaliland independence declaration year: Al Jazeera 1991 vs. World Politics Review 1990 (conventionally recorded as 1991).

Data Caution

Al-Shabaab offensive trends, African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) funding issues, and the identity of the prime minister could not be verified due to search limits. Rural areas controlled by Al-Shabaab are inaccessible for government statistics.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of State (Acting President)Captain Ibrahim Traoré2022-09 (Assumed power via coup; 5-year military rule extension announced in 2024-05)Military transitional government; Rotating Chair of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) (2025-12~)
Head of GovernmentUnidentifiable (Prime Minister's name not listed in collected sources)UnidentifiableUnidentifiable

Base date 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

Captain Traoré suspended political party activities after seizing power in a coup in 2022-09, and extended military rule by 5 years (until 2029) following a national consultation boycotted by the opposition in 2024-05. He expanded the nationwide 'Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP)', a militia established in 2020, pursuing a military-centered counter-terrorism line, while distancing the nation from existing regional and international bodies by withdrawing from ECOWAS in 2025-01 and the Francophonie in 2025-03.

Current Government Direction

The direction is shifting away from a multi-party system (abolition of the Independent National Electoral Commission in 2025-07, dissolution of all political parties in 2026-01), which the government explains as 'national reconstruction' and prevention of division. Externally, the country is strengthening an independent path away from Western-led institutions through the launch of the AES Joint Security Force (2025-12), coordination with Mali and Niger, and the declaration of withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2025-09.

Chronology 2024~2026

  • 2025-01-29Officially withdrew from ECOWAS alongside Mali and Niger.[1]
  • 2025-05-11JNIM seized and attacked the Djibo military base, resulting in approximately 100 deaths (more than 100 civilian deaths were also reported).[1][2]
  • 2025-07-17Abolished the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) and transferred electoral management to the Ministry of Territorial Administration.[1]
  • 2025-09-22Jointly declared withdrawal from the ICC alongside Mali and Niger, citing 'selective justice'.[1]
  • 2025-12-21The AES Joint Sahel Security Force was officially launched.[1]
  • 2026-01-06Minister of Security Mahamadou Sana announced the thwarting of a coup plot led by former transitional president Damiba and funded by Côte d'Ivoire.[3]
  • 2026-01-29The Council of Ministers passed a decree dissolving all political parties and reverting their assets to the state, citing 'division and abuse'.[4][5]
  • 2026-02-12Analyses indicated that more than 130 people died after JNIM launched coordinated attacks across the northern and eastern regions up to 2-22, including the Titao military base (2-15).[6]
  • 2026-07-04JNIM staged coordinated attacks in Di, Solhan, and Séguénéga near Dédougou, killing at least 22 people (AFP, reported as 'Saturday').[7]

Public Trends

With the dissolution of political parties (2026-01) and reports of forced conscription and detention of critics, judges, and journalists under emergency legislation, space for open collective action by the opposition and civil society has shrunk (HRW). In 2025-03, three journalists including the president of the Journalists Association were arrested, and the association was dissolved. No reports of large-scale anti-government protests were gathered within the review period (reports from 2025-01 to 2026-07).

Discrepancies in Figures

The military government has not released the number of fallen soldiers for several years (AFP). In 2026-07, the military announced the 'neutralization of over 400 terrorists' in the Sirba and Sebba areas, but this remains independently unverified. JNIM claimed the killing of dozens of personnel and approximately 50 forestry agents in the Titao and Tangaye attacks in 2026-02. Djibo in 2025-05: approximately 100 dead (WPR) vs. over 100 civilians and about 60 soldiers in the separate Rollo area (Wikipedia).

Data Caution

Analyses indicate that government-controlled areas account for only about one-third of national territory (2025-06), and internally displaced persons are estimated at approximately 3 million. Due to the government's non-disclosure of casualties, conflict statistics rely on ACLED and media compilations. The name of the Prime Minister and developments from 2026-08 to 10 could not be confirmed due to search limits.
